blocking.section: Benchmark methodology (Scenarios: O1, S6; S2 Bundle); Budget philosophy (Budget catalog: PB-11)
blocking.issue: New regression from the L3-3 fix. The benchmark Upstream keeps the default `circuitBreaker`, so O1 cannot reach the in-flight ceiling it tests. Traffic management and resilience sets `maxConnections` to 1,024 in-flight attempts per Upstream per Node, and caps one Endpoint at 50% of that, which is 512. Beyond `maxPendingRequests` (256), it answers 503 `RZ-UP-006` at once. O1a holds each admitted request for 1 s at the mock, so it needs about 20,000 upstream attempts in flight. It gets at most about 768, and the rest fail as `RZ-UP-006`. Active requests then never plateau at 20,000, `RZ-RT-005` never fires, and PB-11's 'excess only as `RZ-RT-005`' cannot pass. S6's 1,000 concurrent streams to one mock provider Endpoint also exceed the 512 per-Endpoint cap.

  loadBalancing: {algorithm: round-robin}
  timeout: 2s" (no `circuitBreaker`); O1: "O1a: mock delay 1 s, 30,000 rps, 150% of what the in-flight ceiling admits" with pass criteria "active requests plateau at 20,000"; PB-11: "excess only as `RZ-RT-005` (target)"; S6: "100 chunks per second on 1,000 streams". Traffic management and resilience: "| `circuitBreaker` limits | `maxConnections` 1,024, `maxPendingRequests` 256 ...", "| `maxPendingRequests` | Waiters for that semaphore ... | 503 `RZ-UP-006` at once |", "An Endpoint holds at most max(8, min(2 × its weighted share, 50%) of `maxConnections`) in-flight attempts".
blocking.fix: Give O1 and S6 an overlay that sets the registered `circuitBreaker.maxConnections` and `maxPendingRequests` fields on the mock Upstream. For O1a, at least 40,000 attempts are needed (target), so one Endpoint's 50% share holds 20,000. Alternatively, list several mock Endpoints, and show the per-Endpoint arithmetic. Add 'zero `RZ-UP-006`' to the O1 and S6 pass criteria. State that the mock host holds 20,000 concurrent upstream connections (target), and note which default-circuit-breaker scenarios, such as S1 and S3, stay below 512 attempts in flight.

blocking.section: Benchmark suite and CI gating (Suite layers: the Latency job time budget)
blocking.issue: The L3-5 fix is incomplete. The document asserts that the Latency job fits Testing's 3-hour limit, but its own run rules overflow the rotation slots. The Duration rule gives each gated scenario 5 head and 5 baseline runs of 180 s, each after a 60 s warm-up. That is 10 × 240 s = 40 minutes per scenario. The 'S3 and S5' slot then takes 80 minutes, and the 'S6, S6n and S7' slot takes 120 minutes, against a 75-minute slot. On an S6 night the job totals 80 + 15 + 120 = 215 minutes, over Testing's 'Longest job 3 hours (target)'. The HTTP/3 variant of S3 (M3) adds another 40 minutes to its slot. Warm-up extensions of up to 180 s per run are not budgeted either; in the worst case they take S1 and S2 alone to 120 minutes.
blocking.evidence: "S1 and S2 A/B: 2 × (10 runs × 180 s + 10 warm-ups × 60 s)   80 min (target)"; "One rotation slot per night                                   75 min (target)"; "S3 and S5 | S5x and G1 | O1 and O2 | C1, C2 and R1 | saturation ladders ... | S4 (M2) | S6, S6n and S7 (M3)"; "**Duration.** Five measured runs of 180 s per scenario and commit (target), interleaved with the baseline in A, B, A, B order"; "**Warm-up.** Each run first offers its rate for 60 s (target), discarded, extended in 30 s steps up to 180 s"; Testing: "| `nightly` | Daily, four parallel jobs | Longest job 3 hours (target) |".
blocking.fix: Give per-slot arithmetic, and keep every slot within 75 minutes (target). For example, allow at most one 40-minute A/B scenario per slot, plus runs with absolute criteria only. Split S6, S6n, S7 and the S3 HTTP/3 variant into their own slots, and restate the rotation period, for example 'every item at least every 12 nights (target)', or move items to `release`. blocking.section: Throughput and resources per core (Throughput targets); Benchmark methodology (Scenarios: S3, O1b)
blocking.issue: S3's saturation contradicts S2's, and O1b is built on the S3 figure. S3 runs the same workload and the same Filter Chain as S2, adding TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2, yet it claims 25% more throughput per vCPU. That would mean 100 µs of CPU per request against S2's 125 µs, with extra work added. No arithmetic explains the gap. An operator who sizes TLS traffic from S3 over-provisions throughput by at least 25%. O1b's 60,000 rps offered load and PB-11's goodput reference both derive from this figure.
blocking.evidence: "| S3 | As S2 with 64 connections of up to 64 streams (target) | As S2 | HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3 on 8443 |"; "| S2 reference scenario | 32,000 rps or more (target) | 8,000 rps or more (target) |" and "| S3 HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3 | 40,000 rps or more (target) | 10,000 rps or more (target) |"; "| CPU per 10,000 rps, S2 | 1.25 vCPU or less (target) |"; O1: "O1b: no delay, 60,000 rps, 150% of S3 saturation".
blocking.fix: Set S3's saturation at or below S2's and show the arithmetic, for example 1.25 vCPU plus TLS record and HTTP/2 framing cost of about X µs per request (hypothesis), giving about 28,000 rps (target). Then recompute O1b's offered rate (150%), the O1b goodput line and PB-11. Alternatively, if 40,000 rps is intended, redefine S3's Filter Chain as S1's, with no Filters, and say so in the Scenarios table.

non_blocking.suggestion: "20,000 rejections/s × 16 µs = 0.32 vCPU ... goodput 92% of saturation" is circular. At 92% goodput (36,800 rps), rejections are 60,000 − 36,800 = 23,200/s, which is 0.37 vCPU (9.3%), for about 90.7% goodput. This still meets PB-11, but the margin is thin; show the converged figure. Also note that the 16 µs is the p50 rejection cost.
